title: Mastercard Opens Its Largest Innovation Centre of Excellence in Asia Pacific to Drive the Intelligence Economy
summary:
Mastercard today opened its largest Innovation Centre of Excellence (ICoE)  in Asia Pacific, creating a new regional hub where financial institutions, merchants, governments and  technology partners can work alongside Mastercard specialists to shape the future of commerce in the  intelligence economy. 
The 7,200+ sq L facility brings together expertise in AI, cybersecurity, customer experience and rapid  prototyping, turning promising ideas into real-world solutions faster. More than 55 specialists are already  working across the ICoE to help partners address emerging challenges, strengthen resilience and create  better digital experiences.  
Mastercard plans to add over 250 specialist roles in Singapore by the end of 2029, expanding the talent and  capabilities needed to advance responsible AI, trusted digital commerce, cybersecurity, data and payments  across the region. 
“Mastercard's Innovation Centre of Excellence brings together banks, merchants, technology companies and  governments to develop and test new solutions. By combining expertise in AI, cybersecurity and fraud intelligence, it will help turn emerging technologies into solutions that businesses and consumers can trust,”  said Dr Tan See Leng, Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry), Singapore, at the  launch. “I hope the ICoE will become a lighthouse for payments innovation in Asia Pacific, where new  solutions are developed and proven in Singapore, before being adapted and deployed across ASEAN, India  and beyond.” 
“Mastercard’s Innovation Centre of Excellence marks a new chapter in our long-standing and mul4-faceted  partnership. By deepening its capabilities in AI, cybersecurity and threat intelligence, Mastercard will tackle  emerging challenges and seize new opportunities across Asia Pacific. Singapore will continue to be a key hub  where companies like Mastercard can innovate and pioneer the next generation of technologies for global  markets, and create high-value jobs for Singaporeans,” said Png Cheong Boon, Chairman, Singapore  Economic Development Board (EDB). 
Bringing together the capabilities to build what’s next 
Designed to evolve with changing technologies, risks and business models, the ICoE brings four  complementary spaces together in one facility: 
• AI Centre of Excellence: advancing responsible AI solutions that can make commerce safer, smarter  and more intuitive, including applications in agency commerce, fraud and scam prevention. • Fusion Centre: bringing together experts across cyber, fraud and physical security to identify  emerging risks, coordinate response efforts and strengthen resilience across the ecosystem. • Mastercard Experience Centre: giving financial institutions, merchants and public sector partners an  immersive way to explore emerging technologies and new possibilities for their businesses. • Makerspace: providing a hands-on environment to rapidly prototype, test and refine ideas,  shortening the journey from concept to reality. 
“Singapore continues to distinguish itself through its ambition, talent and ability to stay ahead of change.  Mastercard has been proud to grow its presence here. This new investment reflects our confidence in  Singapore’s future and Mastercard’s commitment to being a partner for the long term,” said Jon Huntsman,  Vice Chairman and President, Strategic Growth, Mastercard. 
“Asia Pacific is moving quickly into a more intelligent and interconnected economy. The opportunity is to turn  new technology into real-world value, securely and at scale,” said Richard Wormald, President, Asia Pacific,  Mastercard. “The ICoE builds on Mastercard’s longstanding collaboration with EDB and Singapore’s strength  as a proven testbed for innovation. It unites capabilities that traditionally sat apart, supporting the region in tackling shared challenges and moving promising ideas into practice faster.” 
From Singapore, shaping the future of commerce across Asia Pacific 
The opening of ICoE in Singapore comes as businesses across Asia Pacific look to close the gap between  technology experimentation and adoption. By 2030, more than one in 10 online shoppers are projected to  routinely use AI agents to make purchases on their behalf, while US$3 trillion to US$5 trillion in global  consumer commerce could be influenced or orchestrated by agency AI. Realizing this opportunity will  require businesses to deploy new technologies responsibly, with security, governance and human oversight  built in from the outset, particularly in a region where cybercrime already accounts for over 30% of recorded  crime. 
The ICoE will connect Mastercard expertise and insights across more than 40 Asia Pacific markets. From  Singapore, it will develop solutions for the region’s diverse needs, with the potential for the strongest ideas  to scale globally.

title: Singapore, Germany test cross-border payments to reduce settlement risk
summary: Zero-knowledge proofs let each ledger verify the other leg was locked, so neither currency settled unless both did, with no shared ledger or intermediary.
content: Singapore and Germany have successfully tested cross-border payments using zero-knowledge proofs. This innovative approach ensures that neither currency settles unless both are locked, effectively reducing settlement risk. The system allows each ledger to verify the other's transaction securely without requiring a shared ledger or any financial intermediary, paving the way for safer international financial transactions.
content_ta: Singapore மற்றும் Germany நாடுகள் cross-border payments பரிவர்த்தனைகளை zero-knowledge proofs தொழில்நுட்பத்தைப் பயன்படுத்தி வெற்றிகரமாக பரிசோதித்துள்ளன. இந்த புதிய முறையானது, இரு நாடுகளின் கரன்சிகளும் உறுதி செய்யப்பட்டால் மட்டுமே பரிவர்த்தனை நிறைவடைவதை உறுதி செய்கிறது. இதன் மூலம் settlement risk பெருமளவில் குறைக்கப்படுகின்றது. எந்தவொரு இடைத்தரகரும் அல்லது பகிரப்பட்ட ledger-ம் இன்றி, இரு நாட்டு அமைப்புகளும் தங்களது பரிவர்த்தனைகளை பாதுகாப்பாக சரிபார்க்க இந்த முறை உதவுகிறது.

summary: A new law lets Germany's customs agency freeze assets worth more than €100,000 without a criminal case if their origin is in doubt.
content: German lawmakers have backed new powers for the country's customs agency to seize crypto and other assets of unclear origin. Under the legislation, authorities can freeze assets valued above €100,000 without requiring an active criminal case if the source of the funds remains in doubt, aiming to crack down on illicit financial activities.

It brings Bitcoin into environments where speed, capital efficiency, and scale are essential, while maintaining fidelity to Bitcoin’s original principles. There is no second. WBTC stands alone in its role, trusted, verifiable, and engineered for a multichain world. title: One in Three Workers Say Parents Face Greater Barriers to Career Progression
summary:
More than a third (34%) of workers believe working parents face greater challenges progressing in their careers, according to research from European financial technology provider payabl.
The figure rises to 43% among workers aged 18–34, compared with 21% of those aged 55 and over.
The research also highlights differences in perceptions of access to opportunities that can influence progression. Just 35% of women believe men and women receive equal networking opportunities at work, compared with 53% of men.
Almost three in ten women (29%) say childcare responsibilities can limit their ability to network or socialise with colleagues outside working hours. Among workers aged 18–34, this rises to 38%.
Jolita Strasunskaite, Group Chief People Officer at payabl., said: “Supporting working parents needs to go beyond parental leave. An organisation doesn't stand still while someone is away. Teams change, projects move forward and new opportunities emerge. Someone can return on the same salary and into the same role but still feel they have lost confidence, visibility or career momentum.
“Careers aren't built solely through formal promotion processes. Relationships and access to opportunities matter too. Employers need to understand whether their working practices create barriers for people with caring responsibilities.”
payabl. has introduced a dedicated Mum Support Group Programme to support employees through pregnancy, maternity leave, postpartum recovery and their transition back into work.
 
The four-month programme brings together small, confidential groups for specialist-led sessions covering emotional wellbeing, physical recovery, relationships, confidence, parenting and work-life integration. It is open to expectant mothers, employees on maternity leave, those returning to work and mothers of young children.
 
The programme aims to help employees navigate the transition into motherhood while maintaining confidence in their professional lives.
 
The initiative also supports the broader objectives of the EU Pay Transparency Directive, which aims to strengthen equal pay and address gender-based pay inequalities. By helping mothers maintain career momentum and access to professional opportunities, payabl. is taking practical steps to address some of the underlying factors that contribute to the gender pay gap.
 
Strasunskaite added: “A good maternity policy protects someone's employment. Supporting career continuity means thinking about what happens before they leave, while they're away and when they come back.
 
“Employers can't remove every challenge associated with parenthood, but we can make sure work isn't creating additional barriers. Having a child shouldn't unnecessarily mean choosing between being present for your family and continuing to build your career.”

New Xplan AI-enabled capabilities designed around the advice workflow
The first phase of development in Iress’ Xplan Evolution programme focuses on making the power of Xplan easier to access, building on the advice data, workflows, modelling and compliance foundations that advice businesses already rely on.

“Just as importantly, these capabilities build on foundations that advice firms already trust, with security, reliability, permissions, and auditability fundamental to everything we develop. AI has enormous potential to improve productivity in financial advice, but its real value will depend on how effectively it is integrated into the advice journey, while keeping advisers firmly in control."
Iress Group CEO and Managing Director, Andrew Russell, said: "Over the past year, we've been focused on building a stronger, more competitive Iress. We're accelerating the evolution of our products, modernising the user experience and embedding AI directly into the workflows our customers rely on every day.
“Our ambition is straightforward: make financial advice more productive and our customers' businesses more competitive.
“Great specialist financial services software is difficult to build. It requires deep industry expertise, trusted data, sophisticated workflows and the reliability that comes from years of investment. These are significant strengths for Iress, and we're building on them.
“This is not about adding AI for the sake of it. It's about delivering better products that make a measurable difference to our customers. We know trust is earned through delivery, not promises. That's why we're focused on getting these capabilities into customers' hands, listening to their feedback and improving at pace.”

title: Private Rental Costs Increase Faster Than Income Growth, New Report Reveals
summary:
Private rental costs have risen faster than income growth, according to a new report from the UK's largest consumer lending Community Development Finance Institution (CDFI), Salad.
 
The report found that renting privately was the most expensive form of housing. While incomes among private renters increased by 8.7%, housing costs rose at a faster pace, climbing by 9.2%. Private renters also allocated the largest share of their income to housing costs, spending 29.7% of their earnings on rent.
 
Growing pressure facing financially underserved households was also highlighted in the report, with private rental costs among Salad’s data set increasing at more than double the UK average rate of 3.8%. This indicates that households already facing financial strains are bearing a disproportionate share of the rising rental costs.
 
Rising housing costs were not limited to the private rental sector. Housing association rents rose by 6.9%, council rents increased by 9.5%, and monthly mortgage costs climbed by 7.9%, outpacing income growth among mortgage payers which stood at 7.7%. 
 
The findings in the report are based on an analysis of over 87 million financial transactions from 37,937 UK workers spanning 1 September 2025 to 31 August 2026, all who had applied for an affordable loan from Salad. The data demonstrates the change in the costs of housing over the year, during which the Renters' Rights Act came into effect.
 

Craig Pennington, CEO of Salad, commented:
 
"The findings from our report offer unique insights into the financial realities facing tens of thousands of people across the UK. Despite having steady incomes and demonstrating responsible financial behaviour, many are seeing house costs rising faster than their income, placing significant pressure on household budgets.
 
"Our research highlights that financially underserved individuals are feeling the impact most acutely, with many experiencing much steeper increases in housing costs than the wider population. This is why ensuring access to fair, and affordable credit is more important than ever, supporting working households across the UK to maintain financial stability and build long-term resilience.”
 
At least one in three UK adults have difficulty accessing affordable credit from mainstream lenders, despite being able to repay it if they want it. Rather than relying solely on historic credit scores, Salad uses Open Banking technology to assess an individual's current financial circumstances and affordability.
 
Founded in 2018, Salad has lent more than £300 million to over 200,000 customers and earlier this year received a King's Award for Enterprise, recognising its innovation in fair and affordable lending.

title: Open Banking Is Not a European Market – It’s 27 Different Ones
summary:
On paper, Europe has a single open banking framework.
PSD2 created the right for licensed providers to access bank accounts across the EU. SEPA created a single euro payments area. Financial services can passport across borders. From a regulatory perspective the architecture looks harmonised.
But in practice, when it comes to open banking technology providers like Noda, we don’t navigate one European market – we navigate dozens of different infrastructures.
Europe harmonised the right to access bank data, however, it did not harmonise how that access works. 
In this article, I explore what still slows pan-European open banking adoption in practice, and what is needed to make 27 markets feel like one.
Fragmentation was built into the design
This fragmentation, however, is not an accident because PSD2 was a Directive, not a Regulation. That meant each Member State had a right to transpose it into national law under its own supervision. There was no central EU technical authority defining a single API specification. Instead, implementation was left to industry groups and domestic banking communities. This was done deliberately to prevent any one framework from dominating the market, leaving room for healthy competition and innovation.
The Berlin Group became the most widely adopted framework. STET emerged in France and Belgium. Poland developed Polish API, the Czech Republic and others developed their own standards. Even within the same framework, banks retained discretion over implementation choices.
When you decentralise implementation across 27 banking ecosystems, you get 27 interpretations of the same rulebook.
Compare that to the UK, where the Open Banking Implementation Entity (OBIE, now Open Banking Limited) mandated a single technical standard for the CMA9 banks, which together cover the vast majority of personal current accounts. Europe chose a different path – one that reflects its institutional structure.
Neither model is inherently right or wrong but they produce very different operational realities.
Even “one standard” isn’t one standard
Even within the same framework, fragmentation persists. Over 80% of European banks have chosen the Berlin Group standard, which should, in theory, simplify integration for third-party services. However, in reality, two banks claiming the same standard can behave very differently. Optional fields vary. Some banks provide enriched transaction data – merchant names, categories, detailed remittance information; others return minimal booking entries.
Versions are not synchronised. One bank may run v1.3 of a standard, another v1.5 with subtle but important differences.
Authentication flows, error handling, timeout thresholds can all differ. Performance differs – sometimes materially. Even within a single country, APIs can behave differently bank to bank. At a pan–European level, the variability multiplies.
What this means for merchants
For merchants, fragmentation shows up in practical ways.
Conversion rates can vary by bank depending on authentication design and redirect flows. Checkout experiences differ by country. Coverage depth varies, especially in smaller markets where not all banks are equally integrated into open banking ecosystems.
In many countries open banking payments cannot fully replace cards – merchants still need card acceptance to cover long-tail banks or customers whose institutions offer limited API functionality.
While launching open banking in one market can be relatively straightforward, for example in Latvia, where 4 major banks cover the vast majority of personal accounts; scaling across five markets is a different exercise entirely. Quality assurance, monitoring and exception handling grow exponentially with each additional ecosystem.
Why infrastructure layers exist
This complexity explains why specialised open banking infrastructure providers have emerged across Europe. 
Instead of merchants integrating separately with each bank, they integrate once with a single API layer. Behind the scenes, that layer translates different bank “dialects,” normalises statuses and error codes, manages authentication flows and monitors performance across hundreds of connections.
For merchants and consumers this complexity is largely invisible, however, for open banking platforms ensuring that user payment experience is seamless across different banks and countries requires constant maintenance and updates.
This is why very few open banking companies connect directly to banks at scale across all European markets. Many of them focus regionally or combine direct integrations in core markets with partnerships elsewhere.
Depth of coverage matters more than country count – a provider may claim it covers 15 markets but have materially stronger connectivity in only five of them. Where coverage is thin, the impact is direct: users who can't find their bank at checkout might abandon the flow entirely. A long list of markets is only as valuable as the quality of connections behind it.
This is not a weakness of the ecosystem but the natural result of building access rights across a decentralised banking landscape.
Is fragmentation stalling adoption?
It has likely slowed cross–border scaling compared to more centralised models in markets like the UK, India or Brazil. For example, the number of open banking user connections in the UK reached 18.81 million in 2026, which is roughly a third of the adult population, compared to around 64 million open banking users in Europe – just a quarter of the banking population, highly unequal across individual markets.
It is easier to launch open banking in one cohesive ecosystem than across multiple supervisory regimes and technical frameworks. 
Nevertheless, fragmentation should not be confused with failure. The adoption of open banking continues across Europe. The number of third party open banking providers has grown from 79 in 2020 to 554 by the end of 2025. 
Consumer familiarity with bank redirect payments is increasing too. Although there no single pan-European source of data for open banking specifically, markets with strong domestic A2A-based payment methods show rising adoption signals – Spanish Bizum hit 1.237B operations in 2025 (+13.2% YoY), Polish BLIK reached 2.9B transactions, and Sweden's Swish processed 1.1B payments (+4% YoY).
Open banking infrastructure is also maturing, performance is improving, authentication flows are becoming more user-friendly. New regulatory discussions under PSD3 and related initiatives are addressing aspects of reliability and fraud prevention.
Fragmentation reflects Europe’s institutional architecture but not a breakdown of the model itself.
What will actually drive adoption
Europe is unlikely to converge on a single API in the near future. And it may not need to.
Merchants do not require perfect uniformity; what they do require is predictability, reliable uptime, consistent user experience and high acceptance rates. The next phase of European open banking will not be defined by whether every bank uses identical technical fields but by whether the infrastructure delivers dependable outcomes at scale.
To get there, banks must elevate their APIs from "compliance-only" to "commercial-grade" performance, while infrastructure providers must pivot from selling "reach" to delivering resilience – perfecting the orchestration that makes 27 different markets feel like one.

title: What Tech Founders Actually Asked Us in Lisbon: A PayDo Recap
summary:
Web Summit ran in Lisbon from 9 to 12 November. It is one of the largest technology events in the world, and this year around 70,000 people came through: founders, investors, engineers, operators and a good number of people simply curious about what everyone else is building. The PayDo team 
 spent it at booth E451 in Pavilion 4, meeting clients, partners and companies looking for a better way to move money.
The weather had other ideas, and three planned days on the floor turned into two. People arrived at the stand with a purpose rather than wandering, and conversations started close to the point.
A few hundred of them later, a clear picture emerged of what is on people’s minds right now.
The question nobody expects to be a problem
Almost every conversation ended up in the same place. Not pricing. Not features. Geography.
A founder would describe the team: developers in Kazakhstan, a designer in Georgia, contractors in a handful of other places. Then came the part they had clearly explained many times before. Several of the largest providers simply do not work with those countries, so payroll turns into a monthly improvisation, paid through whatever route happens to work that month, with the paperwork never quite matching reality.
These are not obscure markets. They are where a lot of the world’s best engineering talent currently sits. Companies hire there on purpose, and then find that the financial system has an opinion about it.
PayDo does work with those markets. For quite a few visitors, that was the entire conversation.
Unusual is not the same as risky
The second pattern was a genuine surprise, mostly because of how broad it was.
The floor was not only software companies. Travel platforms, marketing agencies, creator businesses, logistics, education, a dozen niches that do not fit any standard category. A striking number of them told the same story about applying for payment accounts: declined, or stuck in review for weeks, with no real explanation.
In most of those cases nothing was happening that a compliance team should worry about. The business just did not resemble the template. Revenue arrived in a shape the model had not seen before. A refund pattern came from a deliberate commercial decision rather than a problem. Nobody at the provider had the time or the remit to look closer, so the file sat.
That gap is a large part of why PayDo was built the way it was. A review that reads the business rather than the category takes a little longer at the start, and it ends in a decision based on how the company actually works.
The part that sounds backwards
Here is what made people lean in, and it is not a technology answer.
Every PayDo client gets a named person. Not a queue, not a chat widget, not an assistant that has learned to apologise in four languages. A manager who knows the business, is reachable by email, messenger or phone, and who stays with the account instead of rotating off it.
Say that to a room full of people who automate things for a living and you brace for scepticism. The reaction was the opposite. Several founders offered some version of the same story: a frozen account, an urgent question, and a week spent re-explaining the same situation to a different agent each time.
Automation is very good at monitoring. Judgement is still a human job, so that is where PayDo puts people.

Built by someone with the same problem
This came up far more often than anyone expected, and it changed the tone of a lot of conversations.
PayDo exists because its founder, Serhii Zakharov, ran into this wall himself. He has built several businesses, one of them in tech, and the payment setup he needed did not exist in a form he could simply buy. So it got built.
People hear that differently than they hear a product pitch. It explains why the roadmap looks the way it does, and why a few decisions that seem inconvenient from the outside were made on purpose.
What visitors said
Two comments shared with permission.
From an IT company with developers in Central Asia: “I was really glad to find out PayDo can send money to Kazakhstan. We have several people working there, and getting their salary to them officially and legally has always been a struggle, because most of the big services do not support that country”.
From a travel agency: “A lot of providers do not like working with us, because of the volume of bookings, cancellations and changes that travel involves. It was great to find a provider with solutions that actually suit how we operate, both on cost and on terms”.
About the stand
Booth E451 in Pavilion 4, built around an idea the team keeps coming back to: payments should be the part of a business that nobody has to think about.
That idea made it into the souvenirs as well. Several hundred new friends and partners went home with a black box put together for exactly that purpose, a small anti-stress kit for people who arrive at an event like this with a full schedule and leave with a longer one. Stress-free is how the team wants the work to feel, and it seemed only fair to hand over a physical version of it.
The boxes went faster than anyone predicted, which is being read as a good sign.
For companies that registered during the event, a dedicated offer is waiting at paydo.com/websummit.
What the team is taking home
Two days, a few hundred conversations, and one theme running underneath nearly all of them. Growing companies are not asking for more payment features. They are asking for fewer obstacles that have nothing to do with their business.
Geography that is not held against them. A review that reads what they actually do. A person who picks up.
None of that is complicated to describe. It is simply rare to find in one place, which is more or less why this company exists.
Thank you to everyone who stopped by the stand. If the team missed you in Lisbon, the conversation is still open via the link.

While this breakthrough represents significant technological progress, experts note that successfully breaking Bitcoin's encryption on a 'Q-Day' would still require roughly 13 million qubits, leaving the cryptocurrency secure for now.

content_ta: வாடிக்கையாளர்களை ஈர்க்கவும் தக்கவைக்கவும் வணிக நிறுவனங்கள் ஆன்லைன் மற்றும் நேரடி விற்பனை செக் அவுட் முறைகளை தொடர்ந்து விரைவுபடுத்துகின்றன. செக் அவுட் செயல்முறைகளில் சிக்கல்களைக் குறைப்பது ஷாப்பிங் அனுபவத்தை மேம்படுத்தினாலும், இது மோசடி செய்பவர்களுக்கு எளிதாக வழிவகுத்து விடுகிறது. கட்டண முறைகள் வேகமாகவும் எளிமையாகவும் மாறும்போது, பாதுகாப்பு அம்சங்கள் தவிர்க்கப்படக்கூடும், இதனால் மோசடி நபர்கள் இந்த அமைப்புகளைப் பயன்படுத்தி எளிதாக குற்றங்களில் ஈடுபட முடிகிறது.

title: OpenAI wallet taps card networks
summary: The artificial intelligence company has created a digital wallet through which its ChatGPT agent can use Visa, Mastercard and American Express.
content: OpenAI has developed a digital wallet that allows its ChatGPT agent to interact with major payment systems. Through this new feature, the artificial intelligence company enables its AI agent to utilize cards from Visa, Mastercard, and American Express for transactions, marking a significant step in integrating AI technology with traditional financial networks.
content_ta: OpenAI நிறுவனமானது தனது ChatGPT ஏஜென்ட் முக்கிய பேமெண்ட் நெட்வொர்க்குகளுடன் இணைந்து செயல்படும் வகையில் ஒரு டிஜிட்டல் வாலட்டை உருவாக்கியுள்ளது. இந்த புதிய அம்சத்தின் மூலம், செயற்கை நுண்ணறிவு நிறுவனமானது தனது AI ஏஜென்ட்டை Visa, Mastercard மற்றும் American Express கார்டுகளைப் பயன்படுத்தி பரிவர்த்தனை செய்ய அனுமதிக்கிறது.

title: Mastercard pilots AI travel purchases
summary: The card network is deploying its technology to validate consumers’ agentic transactions and hide their payment details in the process.
content: Mastercard is piloting a new artificial intelligence system designed to handle travel purchases. The card network is deploying this technology to validate consumers' automated agentic transactions. During the process, the system also hides the users' sensitive payment details, enhancing security for digital bookings and transactions.

title: POS competition lightens up
summary: Point-of-sale service providers are facing less intense competition in the market as venture-funded startups drop away, Shift4's CFO contended last week.
content: Point-of-sale service providers are facing less intense competition in the market as venture-funded startups drop away. According to Shift4's CFO, the competitive landscape has lightened up significantly for established players as newer, venture-backed competitors exit the space or struggle to maintain their market presence.
content_ta: வெஞ்சர் ஃபண்டட் ஸ்டார்ட்அப் நிறுவனங்கள் வெளியேறி வருவதால், பாயிண்ட்-ஆஃப்-சேல் சேவை வழங்குநர்களுக்கு சந்தையில் போட்டி குறைந்துள்ளது.
